claims.claim: xrefs-to 0x020783CC (the arm9 HP-meter trampoline that adds +0x56c and jumps into Grow/0x02078488) confirms exactly 8 static call sites, all inside the ov6 battle overlay, all via 'bl' (direct call, not an indirect/table dispatch). One (0x02158BC0) was already traced in the prior damage-pipeline round; the other 7 (0x02157DC0, 0x021582C4, 0x02159274, 0x021592D0, 0x0215952C, 0x02159668, 0x0215A318) are traced for the first time in this round (see following claims).

Call site 0x02157DC0 lives inside a large (~73-case) jump-table dispatcher at 0x02157A44 that switches on parameter r2 (cmp r2,#0x48; addls pc,pc,r2,lsl#2) and, at entry, saves its 4th parameter r3 into r4 (mov r4,r3). The case at 0x02157DB8-0x02157DC0 loads r0=[r5+0x1b4] (r5 = the dispatcher's 2nd parameter, a character-pointer container, matching the same +0x1b4 convention used by the already-known 25%-check calls in damage-pipeline round1) and sets r1=r4 (the pass-through 4th parameter, i.e. a caller-supplied delta, not locally computed or negated) before calling the trampoline. Two neighboring cases in the SAME table apply the identical r0=[r5+0x1b4]/r1=r4 pattern to two OTHER functions instead: 0x02157DC8-0x02157DD0 calls 0x020781E4 (a distinct 32-bit accumulator on char+0x5c8, unrelated to the Grow/GrowMax Meter pair) and 0x02157E04-0x02157E0C calls 0x020783DC (the +0x558 linked-list walker, see Q3 claims). This shows 0x02157A44 is a generic 'apply-delta-by-opcode' battle-event dispatcher that reuses the same character pointer and the same pass-through delta across several distinct gauge/counter mechanics, rather than being specific to HP.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x02157A44; log r2 (opcode selector) and r3 (delta) on entry across many real battle events to enumerate which opcode IDs route to the HP trampoline (0x20783cc) vs the 0x5c8 counter (0x20781e4) vs the +0x558 list walker (0x20783dc), and whether r3 is ever observed negative (drain) as well as positive (fill) for the HP case.
open_questions: the sign/typical value of r3 as supplied by 0x02157A44's own callers was not traced in this pass (its caller at 0x02159BB8 in ov4 sets up r0/r1 for a different purpose visible in that window; r2/r3 for that specific call were not visible in the disassembled window and require a wider trace)

claims.claim: Call site 0x021582C4 lives inside a second, structurally near-identical jump-table dispatcher at 0x0215807C (selector this time is r3: cmp r3,#0x43; addls pc,pc,r3,lsl#2, using a mix of compare-then-jump-table for the low range). Its case at 0x021582BC-0x021582C4 uses the exact same r0=[r5+0x1b4] / r1=r4 pattern as claim above to call the HP trampoline, and the very next case (0x021582CC-0x021582D4) again applies the same r0/r1 to 0x020781E4 (the char+0x5c8 accumulator), mirroring the case ordering seen in 0x02157A44. This strongly suggests 0x0215807C is a sibling/peer dispatcher to 0x02157A44 (e.g. a different battle-event class using the same underlying opcode table layout), not a separate gauge-specific handler.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x0215807C; log r3 (opcode) on entry across many events and compare against the opcode set seen at 0x02157A44 to determine whether these are truly parallel/peer dispatch tables (e.g. attacker-side vs defender-side) or distinct opcode spaces.

claims.claim: Call sites 0x02159274 and 0x021592D0 are two tiny (7-8 instruction), near-identical wrapper functions (0x02159260 and 0x021592C0) that both take r0=[r0_param+0x1b4] (character pointer, same convention as above) and r1 derived from a signed halfword field two pointer-hops away ([[r1_param+4]+4], read via ldrsh). The ONLY difference between them: 0x02159260 additionally scales this value by 64 (lsl r1,r1,#6) before calling the trampoline, while 0x021592C0 passes it through unscaled. Neither wrapper contains any negation (rsb) instruction, so the sign of the delta is entirely data-driven (whatever sign the source halfword field already has), not hard-coded as a drain by these wrappers.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x02159260 and 0x021592C0; dump the signed halfword at [[r1+4]+4] and its sign across many hits/effects to determine whether this pair implements a x64-scaled 'raw stat to gauge units' conversion (matching the damage-pipeline suggested-next-angle about a x64 multiply) versus the unscaled sibling being a different unit already in gauge units.
open_questions: what object [r1_param+4] points to (a koma/move descriptor?) and what its own +4 field represents numerically

claims.claim: Call sites 0x0215952C and 0x02159668 are two more small wrapper functions (0x02159500, 0x02159624) that gate the HP-trampoline call behind a shared eligibility-check function 0x0215986C: they call it with r2=0x1d (29) and r2=0x1b (27) respectively, and if it returns 0 they skip the trampoline call entirely (movne r0,#0; popne). 0x0215986C itself calls a further predicate 0x2158eb0 on (structBase+0x120, code) and only proceeds (clears node flags, fires effects via 0x215f6e4/0x0207342c) if that predicate is nonzero -- i.e. this is a type/eligibility code (27 vs 29) gating a battle effect, not a different gauge offset. Both wrappers, once past the gate, use the same unscaled r0=[r5+0x1b4]/r1=ldrsh[[r4+4]+4] pattern as claim above. 0x02159624 additionally fires a conditional side-effect call to 0x0215B348 based on a [r4+0xe] flag before applying the delta.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x0215986C; log r5 (char ptr), the r2 code (0x1d/0x1b), and the return of 0x2158eb0(r5+0x120, code) across different attack/status types, to determine what the 27/29 codes select (e.g. elemental type match, guard-break eligibility) and confirm this is orthogonal to which gauge is targeted.
open_questions: semantics of eligibility codes 0x1b/0x1d and of the predicate function 0x2158eb0

claims.claim: Call site 0x0215A318 is inside a large per-character function 0x02159EF8 that begins with a 'run once' sticky-flag check on [r6+0x14] bit0 and performs several capped-increment operations on other fields (e.g. [r2+0x48..0x4c]) -- consistent with a per-frame/per-tick passive update routine. The specific path reaching the trampoline first tests a signed halfword at [r6+0xcc] for nonzero (an enable gate), then unconditionally (regardless of that gate's outcome by the time control reaches 0x215a300) reloads r1 = [[[r6+0x1a8]+0x10]+0x140] and skips the call entirely if that value is 0 (beq), otherwise calls the HP trampoline with r0=[r6+0x1b4] and this r1. Critically, r1 here is NOT negated anywhere in this window (contrast with the confirmed damage-drain call in damage-pipeline round1's claim 6, which explicitly computed r4=-[ptr+0xe8] via rsb before the same trampoline) -- so this is a distinct, sign-agnostic 'apply scratch+0x140 delta if nonzero' pathway on the SAME [[charPtr+0x1a8]+0x10] scratch base already implicated in the damage pipeline (which used +0xe8), now showing a second live field (+0x140) at that base that also feeds the trampoline, most consistent with a passive fill (regen) or damage-over-time tick rather than a one-shot hit.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x0215A308; log [[[r6+0x1a8]+0x10]+0x140] each frame across a match to determine whether it is ever negative (drain, e.g. poison/burn) as well as positive (regen), and whether it correlates with a known equip/status effect (e.g. a life-steal or HP-regen badge).
open_questions: what writes [[charPtr+0x1a8]+0x10]+0x140, and does it represent a per-frame passive HP delta from an equipped item/status effect

claims.claim: The ONLY static caller of 0x02078488 (Grow) OTHER than the already-known trampoline 0x020783CC is the +0x558 linked-list walker 0x020783DC itself: at 0x0207840C-0x02078414 it sets r0=r4 (the CURRENT LIST NODE pointer, obtained by traversing a singly-linked list rooted at [charPtr+0x558]) and r1=r5 (the walker's own 2nd parameter, i.e. whatever delta its caller supplied), then calls Grow directly with 'bl' (not through any offset-adding trampoline). This means the node itself -- at offset 0, not some fixed character-struct offset -- is treated as the Meter base by Grow.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x02078414; confirm r0 is a heap/pool address distinct from the character struct base and distinct from [charPtr+0x56c], and dump r0+0x16/+0x18 before/after the call to confirm it behaves as an independent Meter instance.

claims.claim: The known trampoline 0x020783CC reaches Grow (0x02078488) via an indirect 'bx ip' whose target is an inline pool word (0x02078488, little-endian bytes 88 84 07 02) stored immediately after the trampoline's own 3 instructions, at 0x020783D8. Re-running xrefs-to and pool-values against 0x02078488 in this round both return zero literal_load hits -- i.e. this exact, already-proven-to-exist pool reference is invisible to both of those query.py subcommands. Consequently, any hypothetical SIBLING trampoline elsewhere in the ROM that used the identical 'ldr ip,[pc,#4] / ldr r0,[r0,#OTHER_OFFSET] / bx ip' pattern to jump into 0x02078488 or 0x020784B8 with a base offset other than +0x56c would be similarly invisible to xrefs-to/pool-values searches against those two addresses; no such sibling was found by any method available through query.py in this pass, but this is a demonstrated tooling blind spot, not a proof of absence.
open_questions: a full manual, address-by-address disasm sweep of ov6 (and any other overlay that might host battle logic) for the 3-instruction 'ldr ip,[pc,#4]/ldr r0,[r0,#N]/bx ip' byte pattern was not performed in this pass and would be the definitive way to rule sibling trampolines in or out

claims.claim: 0x020784B8 (GrowMax) has exactly one static caller in the whole database: 0x0215C73C, inside a function at 0x0215C704. That call site tests bit 0x80 of [r4+0x128] (a character status/flags word) and, only if set, calls GrowMax with r0=[r4+0x1b4] (character pointer, same convention as all other sites in this file) and a fixed literal delta r1=0x400 (1024). Since GrowMax's own body (per damage-pipeline round1 claim 5) hardcodes 'ldr r2,[r0,#0x56c]' internally, this caller -- like every other path found in this round -- can only ever grow the +0x56c (HP) meter's max field; no caller-supplied offset mechanism exists for GrowMax, so it structurally cannot reach a second gauge instance without a wholesale rewrite, only a different (unfound) copy of the function.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x0215C73C; check which equip/status effect sets bit 0x80 of char+0x128 (likely an 'HP Up'-style permanent max-HP badge), and confirm the max-HP field at [charPtr+0x56c]+0x16 increases by exactly 1024 when this fires.

claims.claim: Synthesis for Q2: across every statically-reachable call path enumerated in this round (the 8 trampoline sites into Grow, the 1 direct walker call into Grow, and the 1 direct call into GrowMax), no fixed character-struct base offset OTHER than +0x56c was found feeding either accumulator. The one structurally different path is the +0x558 list walker, which supplies Grow with a dynamically-linked NODE pointer (offset 0 relative to the node, not a fixed offset relative to the character struct) rather than any alternate constant offset -- contrast the trampoline's 'ldr r0,[r0,#0x56c]' (fixed offset from character pointer) against the walker's 'mov r0,r4' (r4 = a pointer freshly loaded from a linked list, no offset arithmetic at all). This reframes the search for guard/SP gauges: if they reuse Grow/GrowMax at all, the evidence points toward them being dynamically-allocated list nodes reachable via char+0x558, not additional fixed struct-offset fields analogous to +0x56c.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x02078488 (Grow) globally for one full battle and log every distinct r0 value observed; classify each as either exactly [charPtr+0x56c] (the known HP pointer) or something else (a list node address), to get an empirical count of how many distinct Meter instances actually flow through Grow in practice.

claims.claim: Full body of the +0x558 linked-list walker 0x020783DC: it loads r4 = [r0+0x558] (list head; r0 here is the character pointer, confirmed by this being the SAME r0 passed by callers as [charPtr+0x1b4] in claims above), returns immediately if the list is empty (cmp r4,#0; popeq), then for each node checks two independent skip conditions -- a byte flag at node+0x40 (ldrb r0,[r4,#0x40]; cmp r0,#0; bne skip) and bit 0 of a word at node+0x3c (ldr r0,[r4,#0x3c]; tst r0,#1; bne skip) -- and ONLY IF BOTH flags are clear calls Grow(r0=node, r1=r5=the walker's caller-supplied delta) before advancing to the next node via ldr r4,[r4] (node+0x0 = next-pointer) and looping while r4 != 0.

Answering Q3's flag-semantics question: node+0x3c (bit 0) and node+0x40 (byte) do NOT distinguish node TYPE (e.g. HP-node vs guard-/SP-node) -- both the 'flag set, skip this node' path and the 'flags clear, apply delta' path converge on the exact same single call to 0x02078488 (claim above), with no branch anywhere in this function to any alternate accumulator based on either flag's value. The two flags read as generic per-node ENABLE/PAUSE gates (e.g. 'inactive' and some other lock bit) applied uniformly to whatever node is being visited, not as a discriminator that would let this walker treat different gauge kinds differently.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x020783F4 on every walker invocation for a full match; dump node+0x3c and node+0x40 for every node visited alongside node addresses, to see whether nodes cluster into distinct 'kinds' (by base address/allocator or by a field elsewhere in the node) even though these two flags themselves are not type-selective.
open_questions: how many distinct node 'kinds' actually populate this list at runtime -- unresolved by static analysis of the walker alone, see next claim

claims.claim: Exactly 2 static call sites reach the +0x558 walker 0x020783DC (mirroring the 2 large-dispatcher call sites into the HP trampoline from claims above, out of the trampoline's 8 total): 0x02157E0C (the case in dispatcher 0x02157A44 already shown) and 0x021592B4, inside a tiny wrapper (0x021592A0) that is byte-for-byte identical to the HP-trampoline wrapper 0x02159260 from an earlier claim (same r0=[r0+0x1b4], same r1=ldrsh[[r1+4]+4] scaled by 64 via lsl#6) except its final call targets 0x020783DC instead of 0x020783CC. This confirms the walker is exposed through the SAME generic small-wrapper/dispatch infrastructure as the fixed HP meter, i.e. the two are peer mechanics in the battle-effect opcode system rather than one being a sub-component of the other. Neither call site, nor the walker itself, contains any code that selects among multiple node 'types' -- so how many distinct gauge-node types exist cannot be determined from the call sites or the walker in isolation.
claims.gdb_check: break 0x020783DC across a full match with active guard-break and SP-consuming abilities; log every distinct node address and its node+0x00/0x16/0x18/0x3c/0x40 fields to empirically determine the number and shape of distinct node kinds actually linked into this list, since static analysis found no type-dispatch code to answer this directly.
open_questions: exact count and kind of gauge-node types walked per character -- UNRESOLVED by static analysis in this pass; requires either a runtime GDB census of node addresses/fields or locating the (unfound) constructor/allocator that links new nodes into char+0x558

claims.claim: The list root and 3 adjacent fields (char+0x558, +0x55c, +0x560, +0x564) are zero-initialized together in a single startup loop (arm9, ~0x02075FF8-0x02076008), consistent with +0x558 being a NULL-terminated list head that starts empty per character slot. A global search-imm for immediate value 0x558 across the whole ROM found 37 total load/store hits, of which only ONE is a store (this same zero-init at 0x02075FF8) -- every other reference is a read (ldr). No instruction of the form 'str Rx,[Rbase,#0x558]' that would insert/replace the list head with a non-zero node pointer was found anywhere in the database in this pass (note: a split 'add Rt,Rbase,#0x558' + zero-offset store would not be caught by this immediate-based search, so this is not a proof that no such insertion code exists).
claims.gdb_check: watch [charPtr+0x558] for writes during a full match to catch the actual node-insertion code (likely a 'add Rt,charPtr,#0x558' + register-offset store, invisible to the immediate-based search-imm scan used statically) and identify what allocates/constructs list nodes.
